opinions.basis: Autograph full score inspected pp.1,2,8,16 and engraved first part p.2: exposed high-register runs, sustained fast articulation, chromatic shifts and repeated double-stop/octave passages. Lower parts do not justify an ensemble uplift. Named four-student complete studio performance gives full-work context; seven reflects the first violin with one-level uncertainty.

Actual complete manuscript score inspected across PDF pp.1–3, 6, 8, 12 and 16. Brisk 3/8 scherzo texture alternates repeated semiquaver cells with short slurred chromatic figures, abrupt rests and staggered handoffs. Violin 1 repeatedly reaches well above the staff into the high E-string register and finishes with sustained rapid high repeated figures; several passages in the upper parts include double stops, while lower parts maintain chromatic ostinatos and displaced accents. The persistent high-register articulation and intonation justify pre-diploma level 6, above the level-4 Bach Double anchor and around the broader technical preparation of Mozart violin/viola duos at 6; the notation is substantially less dense than the level-8 Prokofiev two-violin sonata anchor. No automatic ensemble uplift; approximately one-level uncertainty, especially because no numerical tempo is supplied on the inspected opening.

A single 3/8 Scherzo (source42-103548.pdf, Violin I PDF pp.1-3; handwritten score source42-103546.pdf pp.1-6, 14-16). Violin 1 plays fast repeated 16th-note patterns marked ff and fff, with whole bars of slurred repeated notes (PDF pp.1-3) written on four or more ledger lines above the staff, and a closing stretch of about 40 bars of continuous high-register 16ths ending on sustained very high notes. The part also contains long stretches of metrically displaced rests and rapid chromatic cells. The lower parts (handwritten score) use dense 16th-note repeated-note ostinati and pitch-displaced figures. Extreme high-position security and endurance plus tight rhythmic interlock are what lift it. The handwritten score is hard to read, so some details are inferred from the engraved Violin I part.

Complete 17-page Namba score; inspected pp.1,4,8,12,14,17: first cello sustained tenor-register melody, chromatic slurred semiquaver runs, displaced figures and double stops, with lower parts generally less exposed. Named complete Op.28 2002 Casals Hall concert provides full-work context. Six reflects the individual first part, without ensemble uplift; plausible one-level uncertainty.

Actual complete score inspected at PDF pp.1–2, 4–5, 8, 12 and 17: the first cello moves repeatedly between bass and tenor clefs into the singing upper register, with extended slurred semiquaver passagework, chromatic inflections, ornaments and register changes. Allegro moderato and Allegretto variations add detached articulation and coordinated short rests; the lower three parts also exchange moving figures, while the return to Andante requires exposed sustained ensemble intonation. This is advanced cello work around the ABRSM 8 / RCM 9 band (level 5), above the uncomplicated intermediate Telemann four-violin anchor at 2, but without the sustained virtuoso density of diploma-level chamber anchors. No automatic ensemble uplift; approximately one-level uncertainty from representative distributed inspection.

A theme with variations in a notation-program score (source42-617255.pdf). Cello 1 reads bass, tenor and alto clef in alternation and plays in upper positions with fluent 16th-note runs and turns (PDF pp.1-6), 6/8, 2/4 and 3/4 contrasts, a Maestoso with chordal figures (PDF p.9), an Andantino and a Scherzando in 6/8 (PDF pp.10-12), and ending on sustained dynamics (PDF p.17). The material is regular and imitative; the tenor-clef upper register and the sixteenth runs are the highest hurdle for cello 1, so it sits at the early advanced end with ordinary ensemble demands.

Complete 14-page score and parts; inspected title, score opening, first-cello p.7 and fourth-cello p.14: high tenor/treble cantabile, slurred chromatic flourishes and large shifts, including an unexpectedly high fourth-cello passage. First cello remains most exposed over whole work. RADIX live-concert upload supplies full-work context. Six, with one-level uncertainty, without ensemble uplift.

Actual complete score (PDF pp.2–3) and both first-cello part pages (pp.7–8) inspected. The Adagio introduction contains chromatic slurred semiquaver runs and accented detached figures; Allegro moderato (quarter=120) requires sustained upper-register tenor-clef cantabile, expressive shifts, harmonics and occasional double stops, followed by Meno mosso passagework and an exposed soft ending. The score also shows fourth-cello ascending chromatic/arpeggiated excursions, though the first part has the most sustained high melodic responsibility. Advanced level 5 (ABRSM 8 / RCM 9 equivalent on cello) fits these demands: more than early-advanced 4 lyrical chamber parts, below the continuous technical breadth of pre-diploma 6 anchors. Exposed tuning/balance does not itself add a level; approximately one-level uncertainty.

Single-movement Elegie in an engraved full score plus viola parts (source42-10006.pdf, PDF pp.2-3, 5-6). Cello 1 is in tenor clef in a high but moderate register (up to about C or D above the staff), mainly slurred quarter and 8th-note phrases, a few short 16th-note groups and a short chromatic passage, with the Allegro moderato in D major quite regular. Cello 4 has a short rising 16th-note run in positions 1-4 (PDF p.3, bottom staves) and pizzicato bass. The main demands are tenor-clef reading, intonation and phrasing, with the Meno mosso section requiring balance across four equal voices.
